text:
The data never stops arriving. Clicks, payments, sensor readings: the stream has no last row to wait for. Streaming interviews test how Kafka, a distributed log, spreads it across machines, what a delivery guarantee really promises, and how to count over time when events arrive late and out of order. Fifteen questions: twelve worked through, most on one small stream of the video's own, twelve clicks from four users, then three quick ones.

Question one. What are Kafka topics, partitions, and offsets? A topic is a named log that only grows at its end. It's split into partitions, the unit of parallelism. Each message gets an offset: its position in its partition, counting up from zero. The producer hashes each message's key to pick a partition, so all of ava's clicks land in one, in the order they arrived. Order holds inside a partition, never across them. A message with no key goes round-robin. Question two. Why does the number of partitions matter in Kafka? Partitions cap how many consumers can share the work, and set where order holds. More of them buy throughput, at a cost: more open files, longer rebalances, more latency. You can add partitions later but never remove them, and adding them moves keys. Model it with ten thousand keys, hashed into three partitions, then four: seventy-four percent move, so a user's new clicks can be read before their old ones. Size for peak, with headroom.
